mcqs.question: Why does the model need both a Book and a separate BookItem class instead of one Book class?
options: Because relational databases require every entity to have at least two related tables
Because Book is only used for e-books and BookItem is only used for physical copies
Because Member objects can only reference BookItem, never Book, for security reasons
Because BookItem holds per-copy state (condition, barcode, status) while Book holds shared catalog data, and availability must be tracked per physical copy
mcqs.explanation: Book vs BookItem exists to separate shared catalog data (title, author, ISBN) from independent per-copy state (which exact copy, its condition, who holds it). There's no database rule forcing this split, both classes apply to physical books here, and there's no security reason for the reference direction.

mcqs.question: Why does this design use Strategy for fine policy but deliberately skip Observer for hold-ready notifications?
options: Strategy removes a growing if/else across member types, while a periodic scheduled job already satisfies the not-latency-sensitive notification requirement without added machinery
Observer is deprecated in modern object-oriented design and should never be used
Strategy and Observer solve the same problem, so only one may be used per design
Fine calculation cannot be represented as an interface, only as conditional logic
mcqs.explanation: The two decisions are independent: Strategy earns its place because fine rules genuinely vary by member type and keep growing, while a scheduled job is simpler than wiring up Observer for a notification that isn't time-critical. Observer isn't deprecated, and fine calculation is exactly the kind of thing Strategy interfaces represent well.

mcqs.question: A popular title's last checked-out copy is returned and three members are waiting on holds. What should happen?
options: The copy becomes generally AVAILABLE immediately, first-come-first-served
The copy moves to ON_HOLD for the front of the FIFO queue, with an expiry window before it can go to general availability
The copy is deleted and a new BookItem is created for the next holder
All three waiting members are notified simultaneously and whoever checks out first gets it
mcqs.explanation: Holds exist precisely so the person who has been waiting longest gets first refusal, not whoever happens to check next. The item goes ON_HOLD for the front of the queue with an expiry, only falling back to general availability if that member doesn't claim it in time. Notifying everyone at once defeats the purpose of a FIFO queue.

mcqs.question: Two members try to check out the last available copy of a title at nearly the same instant. What actually prevents both from succeeding?
options: Making the checkout button disabled for 2 seconds after any click
Re-checking availability in the UI five seconds after checkout completes
An atomic conditional update (e.g. UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE') where only the request that actually changes a row wins, rather than a separate read-then-write
Limiting the library to only one member logged in at a time
mcqs.explanation: A read-then-write checkout lets both requests read AVAILABLE before either writes, so both think they succeeded. Only collapsing the check and the write into one atomic conditional operation guarantees exactly one request's update actually takes effect. UI delays and post-hoc re-checks don't close the race window.
